implementation_notes: The JDK defines the pattern: java.io.Serializable, Cloneable and RandomAccess are empty interfaces that the serialization runtime, Object.clone() and the Collections algorithms test with instanceof or a generic bound - the Serializable javadoc states that the interface has no methods or fields and serves only to identify the semantics of being serializable. Declare an empty interface, let marked classes implement it, and gate behaviour with instanceof or a type parameter. Annotations have largely replaced markers for descriptive metadata, but the classic form remains the right choice when the mark must constrain method signatures, generic bounds or pattern matches, which annotations cannot do. The mark is inherited by every subclass and cannot be removed, so a subclass that cannot honour it must fail explicitly (NotSerializableException).
pitfalls: The mark is inherited by all subtypes and cannot be unimplemented; a subclass that cannot honour it must throw a documented runtime failure.
Markers cannot carry values or target methods and fields - annotations are needed there.
java.io.Serializable is a known deserialization attack surface: the Java 21 javadoc warns that untrusted data must be validated or avoided.

variants.name: Marker annotation plus reflection
variants.idiom_name: @interface with no elements, read via reflection
variants.implementation_notes: Since Java 5 an annotation can carry the same fact with values and can target types, methods, fields and parameters; a marker annotation with no elements is metadata inspected by reflection or an annotation processor. Annotation checks happen at run time (or at build time via processors) and never constrain a method signature - Effective Java Item 41's rule is to use a marker interface exactly when you might write a method that accepts only marked objects. Prefer annotations when the signal is descriptive, carries attributes, or must be consumed by tooling.
pitfalls: Annotation checks are a run-time decision (or a build-time processor), so a missing annotation is not a compile error.
@Inherited is opt-in and only applies to class annotations; interface implementation has no such subtlety.
Reflection-based annotation lookups are slower than an instanceof test and are normally cached.

variants.name: Sealed interface and records for a closed marked set
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface with permitted records and exhaustive switch
variants.implementation_notes: When the marked set is closed and known, a sealed interface listing its permitted implementations plus an exhaustive switch gives the compiler the complete case list; this replaces markers that existed only to enumerate a set and removes the runtime tag test. It cannot model open, cross-library categories, where a plain marker interface remains correct, and every exhaustive switch must be revisited when the permitted set changes.
pitfalls: Sealed permits form a closed set: adding a case changes every exhaustive switch at compile time - intentional, but it is churn.
Permitted subtypes must be in the same module and package (or declare themselves), which constrains module layout.
Sealed is about case analysis, not about a boolean fact; do not use it where the category must stay open.
